The Assembly will consider in a joint debate agenda item 28, entitled Report of the Peacebuilding Commission, agenda item 62, entitled Peacebuilding and Sustaining Peace and Agenda Item 112, entitled Report of the Secretary-General on the Peacebuilding Fund. The documentation under these items is listed in the Journal of the United Nations. I now make a statement as the President of the General Assembly. Excellencies, Tomorrow we commemorate 81 years since the signing of our United Nations Charter. The Charter is both a promise and a warning. It gives form to our aspiration for a better future while reminding us of the horrors we endured to learn the hard lessons. Peace does not occur automatically. It is built through persistent diplomacy collective action and political will. 8 decades on, we should be alarmed at our trajectory. The number of active armed conflicts reached a record high in 2025, and nearly 40% of countries emerging from conflict relapse within 5 years. Meanwhile, between 2024 and 2025 alone, global humanitarian funding collapsed by 40%. This is despite what our 8 decades of United Nations efforts to maintain peace, prevent conflict, and support recovery have taught us: that peace and security, sustainable development, and human rights are inseparable. We meet at a moment of cynicism. Some complain that the United Nations is not doing enough to deliver peace. And security. Even if we fail to invest sufficiently in the foundations of peace and the institutions that support it. When institutions are weak, grievance grows. Where justice is delayed, trust erodes. And where the rule of law is ignored, nationally or internationally, instability spreads and development becomes harder to sustain. We are often asked by the public and journalists alike whether the United Nations is still worth it if it cannot end the devastating wars currently underway. Yet wars that never happen because of these efforts, because of our peacebuilding efforts, because of conflict prevention or sustainable development, rarely make headlines. Unfortunately, there is no glory in prevention. Yet, we know prevention and peacebuilding is the most noble things to ensure peace. Saving succeeding generations from the scourge of war therefore means first and of all valuing peacebuilding and conflict prevention as a core part of the work of the United Nations. And for sure and without doubt, We all have to do better to bring peace to the war zones, to Sudan, Ukraine, Gaza, and Lebanon, and to conflicts that too often escape global attention, including in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, or the situation in Haiti and elsewhere. Yet, we should also value the successes which are there, but as said, unfortunately, hardly make headlines, such as in Central Asia, where Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan have engaged on transboundary water issues intensively, and the empowerment of women and regional cooperation backed by the United Nations Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy not only solved a year-long struggle around borders, but also going forward on water management. Building peace, building trust, preventing further crisis—this is preventive diplomacy across the region. This is the core of the work we are doing here for 8 decades. In the Pact for the Future, therefore, member states committed to strengthening preventive diplomacy and dialogues between states. The Pact recognizes the importance of national efforts to sustain peace and enhance international security, while also pledging to give the Peacebuilding Commission a more strategic role. Furthermore, the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review, adopted in November by the General Assembly and the Security Council, builds on 20 years of experience to strengthen the impact of peacebuilding efforts. That experience includes— further successes, for example in Liberia, where after 14 years of civil war, the Commission supported national efforts on transitional justice and the women and youth agendas. It is another powerful reminder of what can be achieved when peacebuilding is treated as a core priority. Yet, like everything else, peacebuilding is only possible when properly resourced. The Pact therefore affirms that member states bear the primary responsibility for preventing conflict and building peace in their own countries and supports nationally owned efforts. But national ownership does not mean countries should carry these burdens alone. External support remains essential. And the Peace Building Fund is exactly the tool leading to this aim. Since 2006, the Peacebuilding Fund has supported 75 countries and territories and invested more than $2 billion, sustained by the voluntary generosity of more than 60 Member States. For example, the PBF became the first contributor to the UN Multi-Donor Trust Fund in Colombia, which has mobilized more than $217 million for the implementation of the 2016 peace agreement. This is the core work of the United Nations—preventive diplomacy, peacebuilding at its heart. In the Central African Republic, the Fund supported the 2025-2026 electoral cycle, including presidential, legislative, regional, and municipal elections. The completion of that cycle marked an important step towards extending government authorities across the country. It has also helped widen political participation, with women making up 45% of elected municipal councillors, including the newly elected mayor of Bangui. This shows again how our work on peace is deeply interconnected with delivering on our SDGs. The goal on strengthening public institutions justice as a core for peace. And we all know these resources work best when they build upon and work in concert with national strategies. Therefore, this first Peacebuilding Week is our chance to show that peacebuilding achieves and to rally the support it deserves, knowing that we are always better together. I thank you. I now give the floor to the former chair of the Peacebuilding Commission, the distinguished representative of Germany.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, let me begin by conveying my sincere appreciation to you for convening this important debate and for giving me the opportunity to address the General Assembly. It's a privilege to speak in my former capacity as Chair of the Peacebuilding Commission during its 19th session in 2025. I extend my sincere appreciation to the delegations who served as vice chairs in 2025—Brazil, Japan, Morocco, and Poland—and to all members of the Commission for their strong partnership and commitment. I also wish to thank the United Nations Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office for its tireless and indispensable support throughout the year. 2025 was a— consequential year for the Peacebuilding Commission. It coincided with the 2025 review of the United Nations peacebuilding architecture, providing an important opportunity not only to reflect but to strengthen the way we deliver peacebuilding support across the system. Against this backdrop, the Commission delivered a dynamic program of work. It convened meetings across country-specific, regional and thematic tracks, deepening engagement on situations where sustained international attention is critical to build peace and prevent a relapse into conflict. Furthermore, the Commission supported peacebuilding priorities in countries such as the Central African Republic, Mauritania, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Chad, Columbia, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan, focusing on issues ranging from electoral processes and transitional justice to social cohesion, inclusive governance, peaceful border settlements, and post-conflict recovery. This included field visits, such as the one to Columbia in August 2025, which was conducted with a view to assessing progress in on the implementation of the 2016 peace agreement and broader national peacebuilding priorities, and to provide political accompaniment. Through engagements with national authorities, civil society, former combatants, and members of the diplomatic corps, the delegation gained a deeper, context-specific understanding of outstanding implementation achievements and challenges and identified ways in which the PBC can further support Colombia's peacebuilding efforts, as well as creating means to learn from the capacities built by Colombian entities and civil society in this regard. One of the key achievements of 2025 was the strengthening of the Commission's advisory role. The Commission provided substantive written advice to the Security Council on critical issues, including adaptability in peace operations, local electoral processes, and women, peace, and security. It also increased its engagement with the General Assembly and ECOSOC, demonstrating its growing role as a bridge across the United Nations system. Relations with the African Union remained a priority during the last session. In November 2025, the Commission visited Addis Ababa to participate in the 8th Annual Joint Consultative Meeting with the African Union Peace and Security Council, marking a significant milestone in advancing UN-AU cooperation on peacebuilding. The meeting provided a platform for strategic dialogue on shared priorities for building and sustaining peace in Africa. Through these consultations, both bodies strengthened mutual understanding of their respective roles and comparative advantages while identifying practical avenues for closer coordination, including enhanced information sharing and more coherent support to countries on their agendas. Equally important was the Commission's progress in enhancing its convening role. In 2025, it brought together a wide range of actors—member states, regional organizations, international financial institutions, civil society, and local peacebuilders—around shared peacebuilding priorities. The expansion of partnerships, including strengthened collaboration with international financial institutions, enabled more coherent and integrated responses to complex challenges. Another significant achievement was the Commission's engagement with women peacebuilders across its meetings, reflecting a firm commitment to advancing the Women, Peace and Security Agenda at the eve of the 25th anniversary of Security Council Resolution 1325 last year, and ensuring that women's leadership and perspectives remain central to peace efforts. The Commission also discussed its Gender Strategy and Youth Action Plan, and I am pleased to report that women peacebuilders participated in more than 63% of the Commission's ambassadorial-level meetings. The Commission also made important strides in strengthening its working methods, enhancing flexibility, improving follow-up, and ensuring greater accountability for results. It increasingly demonstrated its added value as a platform for sustained political accompaniment and for mobilizing support for nationally owned peacebuilding priorities. Germany remains firmly committed to supporting peacebuilding and to strengthening the peacebuilding architecture. As we look ahead, our collective task is clear: to translate the outcomes of the review into concrete action and to ensure that the Peacebuilding Commission is fully equipped to deliver on its mandate. And let us always keep in mind that the value of our activities here in New York— convening, advising, accompanying, and coordinating— is measured by concrete peacebuilding outcomes at the country level. Allow me to conclude by extending my best wishes to the current Chair of the Peacebuilding Commission, the Permanent Representative of Morocco, His Excellency Ambassador Omar Hilal. I look forward to continuing our close partnership with him, with all the members of the Commission, and with the United Nations Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office. Together, we have the opportunity and the responsibility to ensure that the promise of sustaining peace becomes a reality for all. Thank you very much.
I thank the former chair of the Peacebuilding Commission. I now give the floor to the current chair of the Peacebuilding Commission, the distinguished representative of Morocco.

Madame la Présidente. Madam President.

Your Excellencies, dear colleagues. It is a great honor for the Kingdom of Morocco to take the floor as chair of the Peacebuilding Commission. In a discussion that is of particular importance this year, we are marking the 20th anniversary of the new UN architecture on peacebuilding, two decades in which we have seen that the situation has evolved considerably. And I would like first of all to hail the key role of Germany and my predecessor in particular the former PR during the 19th meeting of the Peacebuilding Commission. We were grateful to him for his skillful steering of the commission, and we would like to thank him this year for his role as vice chair. I would also like to pay tribute to Brazil and Bangladesh, Inter Alia, for their roles as vice chairs this year. We'd also like to thank all members of the Commission this year for their unwavering commitment to our common agenda. I'd also like to thank the PBSO for their unwavering support to the strategies that we have been implementing. Madam President, we are meeting at a highly symbolic time. At the first Peacebuilding Week, the topic of which highlights the 20 years that have elapsed since the new strategy was rolled out. This initiative bears witness to the commitment to peacebuilding and it offers a precious opportunity for us to deepen our dialogue and partnerships within the United Nations system and and beyond. Since the beginning of our chairmanship, Morocco has been guided by a conviction that the PBC must remain strategic, relevant, and must achieve results in its work. In this regard, our Commission needs to consolidate its advisory role. We have referred opinions to the General Assembly and the Security Council in line with its singular vocation to build bridges between these main bodies of the United Nations. We have also transmitted views to the General Assembly and during the briefing that we made to the Security Council, We spoke about the situation in the CAR. We spoke about the importance of accountability and the rule of law, as well as transitional justice mechanisms, which are critical to peacebuilding. We have also spoken to the General Assembly about the causes of conflicts and promoting sustainable development and peace in Africa, and we invited partners within the United Nations system and international financial partners and development banks to better coordinate their efforts to build peace in Africa and to focus on defined priorities as states have supported at the regional level. One of the key priorities for us has been to further strengthen the way in which the Commission can gather people together focusing on national ownership, targeted discussions on countries such as The Gambia and São Tomé and Príncipe. We have also highlighted the importance of prevention efforts which must be led at the national level and then supported at the international level. We have also spoken about the importance of continued support from the PBC in all of these contexts. We have focused on the importance of visits on the ground in CAR and Liberia, which were unique opportunities for us to engage in direct dialogue with national authorities and local stakeholders and also to measure the progress that has been made and difficulties encountered and build synergies, more robust synergies between the Peacebuilding Fund and the Peacebuilding Commission and finally to reaffirm the need to strengthen national institutions to build on democratic achievements and to ensure that peace can win out in the long term and that countries don't lapse back into conflict. The meeting on women, peace, and security held on the margins of the CSW in March had representatives from Kyrgyzstan, Colombia, and Nigeria. We spoke about the importance of DDR in Telia, and this showed the importance of anchoring our discussions in the lived experience of citizens in those countries. This showed the value of an inclusive approach to peacebuilding led by countries themselves. Our partnerships with the Peacebuilding Fund have also continued to be strengthened through the second annual strategic dialogue, which focused on complementarity between their respective roles, the Commission and the Fund, and also catalytic financing for countries' priorities. National experiences have showed the results that such coordinated approaches can achieve. In addition to this, our work with the World Bank has highlighted the importance of close cooperation with finance— international financial institutes as well. Looking to the future, we remain committed to continue this momentum. We are continuing the implementation of our ambitious program of work by strengthening our partnerships with the African Union Peace and Security Council. And this is in the context of our 8th dialogue that was held in Addis Ababa, and a high-level dialogue that will be held at the next United Nations General Assembly, which will focus on this issue in September. We will also continue to take inspiration from the relevant resolutions of the PBR looking towards 2027, and we will continue to work closely with member states to Member States to move forward the implementation of the conclusions of that review to further bolster the architecture. We are facing an increasingly complex environment, and in this context, the PBC's role is more important than ever. By working with national authorities, the United Nations system, regional organizations, civil society organizations, and international financial institutions, we will be able to move forward more coherent, more inclusive, and more effective agendas to make peace long-lasting. And we should never forget that the value of our activities here in New York are to provide advice, to provide support and coordination for these measures to obtain tangible results on the ground for people. We need to continue this momentum by working with all members and all countries within the United Nations. Madam President, over the last 20 years, we have promised that no post-conflict country will be left in the lurch. This anniversary that we're marking here this week should not just be a commemoration, but rather an opportunity for us to reaffirm this promise and this collective commitment. I thank you.

Thank you, President, and colleagues. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of Australia Canada, and New Zealand. We welcome this debate marking the inaugural United Nations Peacebuilding Week. Conflict prevention and peacebuilding lie at the very heart of the United Nations' purpose. For two decades, the United Nations peacebuilding architecture has demonstrated its value by supporting nationally owned pathways to peace. But today, amid rising conflict and compounding global risks, We must use this architecture more strategically, more consistently, and with greater ambition. To this end, CANZ makes 3 points today. First, we must make better use of the Peacebuilding Commission. The Commission is uniquely placed to provide sustained political accompaniment to nationally-led peacebuilding efforts and to keep international attention on at-risk situations. It brings coherence across the United Nations system, enabling peace and development actors to work more effectively on the ground. We welcome the Commission's growing engagement with the Security Council and ECOSOC, particularly where this strengthens their impact. The Commission should also be used systematically to advance inclusive peacebuilding by ensuring that women, youth, and indigenous peoples can meaningfully contribute to peace processes. Second, sustaining peace requires predictable financing. In 2025, the Peacebuilding Fund supported 48 initiatives across 28 countries, reducing conflict risks, supporting transitions, and advancing nationally-led prevention efforts. From addressing regional conflict dynamics in Papua New Guinea, to reducing vulnerability to gang violence in Haiti, and supporting cross-border initiatives in The Gambia and Senegal, the Fund has shown what targeted, flexible financing can achieve. But demand continues to outpace resources. If we are serious about prevention, we must invest in it. We call on all member states in a position to do so to increase their support to the Peace Building Fund. Third, we must invest earlier and more deliberately in conflict prevention. Today's conflict drivers—climate change, food insecurity, and economic shocks—are accelerating instability, often across borders. Prevention is the most effective and cost-efficient response. The Peacebuilding Commission provides a platform to help countries identify risks early, develop voluntary national prevention strategies to respond more effectively, and mobilize support across the United Nations system and with regional partners. Used in this way, the Commission can shift our collective approach from reaction to prevention. Peacebuilding is not a short-term endeavor.— it's a long-term commitment. If we invest early in prevention, through a stronger Peacebuilding Commission and a fully resourced Peacebuilding Fund, we can shift decisively from reacting to crises to our work to prevent them. Australia, Canada, and New Zealand stand ready to support this effort.

Thank you. I thank the distinguished representative of Australia. On behalf of CANZ, I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union. On behalf of the EU and its member states.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honour to speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states, the candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, Ukraine, The Republic of Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, as well as Armenia and San Marino aligned themselves with this statement. I stand before you today with a profound sense of responsibility and hope as I address the General Assembly during this first-ever Peacebuilding Week. Last year's Peacebuilding Architecture Review reconfirmed our commitment to maintaining peacebuilding as a global priority. The European Union has deeply engaged in the peacebuilding architecture review process and continues supporting the ongoing UNAD process. Our key focus now is its implementation. One critical lesson from the review is the urgent need to communicate more effectively about the positive impact of peacebuilding. Peacebuilding. The Peacebuilding Week marks an important step forward. To support implementation, we have launched a year-long series of EU-supported events that will produce cross-regionally anchored policy recommendations on UN peacebuilding and conflict prevention by early next year. We particularly welcome the strengthened interaction between the Peacebuilding Commission and the UN Security Council enhancing the PCPBC's advisory role. This cooperation is essential as we confront a world marked by spreading conflicts, deepening fragility, lives disrupted, futures stolen, and communities torn apart. This reality also reminds us that peace is not merely the absence of war, but the presence of justice, of opportunities, of enjoyment of human rights and inclusive governance. The Peacebuilding Architecture Review and the Peacebuilding Fund's annual report confirm what we know: prevention works, partnerships matter, and investing in peace saves lives and resources. The European Union was built on the ashes of war, forged from the belief that peace is not inevitable, but a choice we must make every day. Today, as a Union of 27 democracies, We remain committed to that founding principle. We are not just observers of this global challenge, we are active participants in the solution. Let me highlight today 3 key areas where our partnership with the United Nations is making a difference. First, on prevention. The PBAR recognizes that prevention is not just desirable, it is very cost-effective. For every dollar invested in prevention, we save $7 in post-conflict reconstruction. Investing in conflict prevention saves lives and fosters development. To support this, the EU has developed a robust early warning and conflict analysis methodology that enhances our ability to act before conflicts escalate. Secondly, partnerships. The report before us shows that no single actor can address all these complex challenges alone. This is why we as a Team Europe address these issues together. The Peace Building Fund is an example whereby the EU and its member states have so far contributed €630 million to the PBF, and we remain the main contributor. Since inception, we have provided more than 80— 60% of total funding. The PBF has proven to be a valuable instrument in the support of coordinated efforts across humanitarian, development peace nexus. The PBF's catalytic capability must be further leveraged by reinforcing partnerships also at the local level with civil society and regional organizations, with the private sector and international institutions. In the context of the current funding crisis, we must make the best use of funds available. The EU-UN Strategic Partnership on Peace and Security, launched last year, strengthens this work on common priorities such as conflict prevention, mediation, peacebuilding, and peace operations. Third point on innovation. The PPF's focus on cross-border and regional approaches reflects our shared understanding that conflicts do not respect borders. The EU is committed to supporting innovative approaches, but we must do more. First, we have to scale up prevention efforts by investing in early warning systems and inclusive dialogue processes. Second, we have to strengthen further national ownership of peacebuilding processes by supporting local peacebuilders and ensuring the full, equal, and meaningful participation of all segments, segments of society, especially women and youth. And third, enhance UN cohesion and integrated delivery on the ground. By breaking down silos between humanitarian, development, and peacebuilding efforts. This is also recognized in the EU's most recent policy and our documents, the EU Communication on Humanitarian Aid and its renewed integrated approach to fragility. Peace is not a given. It requires courage, commitment, and immediate action. The reports before us are not just documents, they are calls for action. Let us answer those calls together. The EU unwaveringly stands to this multilateral system based on international law, and it stands with the UN at its core. And we remain firm in this. We will continue to strongly support peacebuilding and conflict prevention, as well as the UN's efforts in this regard. Our commitment translates into concrete actions and support. In conclusion, Let me stress once more: together, in partnership, we can deliver on peacebuilding and sustaining peace. Both lie at the heart of both the UN and the EU. The UN can count on the European Union also in the future. Thank you very much.

It is our joint responsibility in this context to urgently find common ground through the ongoing UN reform process, including strengthening the UN's essential and the UN's unique responsibility to maintain and to sustain peace. Excellencies, it is equally important to publicly recognize and acknowledge all the great work that UN personnel provide every day, every hour to advance peace. A lot of the precious work that UN colleagues do actually goes unnoticed. It is difficult to document and it's very hard to communicate that conflicts have been prevented and that peace actually has been sustained. But even in a time of record-high levels of conflict, we know that peacebuilding and prevention efforts actually make a difference. And it works. As evidenced by the breadth of peacebuilding initiatives highlighted under this inaugural Peacebuilding Week, the UN and partners deliver daily and can do more. Both the Pact for the Future and the twin PBAR resolutions adopted last year both give us a shared strategic direction. Our evidence-based toolbox for peacebuilding and sustaining peace is operational and it's ready to be scaled up to meet increasing needs around the world. The advisory The bridging and the convening roles of the Peacebuilding Commission remains essential and crucial in this regard. This toolbox also includes peace mediation, which is essential to make and sustain peace and to prevent conflict from reigniting. Excellencies, reform is critical for effective delivery But adequate, sustained, and predictable financing is equally important. We all know that conflict prevention is cost-effective. Every dollar spent on prevention has significant returns and will save dollars in the future. We should prioritize resources to support inclusive, nationally-owned and led peacebuilding efforts. And preventive diplomacy. In this regard, partnerships are essential, including with civil society, women's groups, and youth organizations, and of course, the IFIs.
