I am honored to deliver this statement on behalf of the group of the Gulf Cooperation Council states, namely the United Arab Emirates, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the Sultanate of Oman, the State of Qatar, the State of Kuwait, and my country, the Kingdom of Bahrain. At the outset, we extend our thanks to the Chair of the Peacebuilding Commission, His Excellency Ambassador Omar Hilal, and we thank Germany for its presidency. We also welcome the report of the Secretary-General on the Peacebuilding Commission and the Peacebuilding Fund. Madam President, the GCC countries believe that investing in peacebuilding and prevention is the most effective way to prevent conflicts by addressing their root causes. The group reaffirms its continued support for the Peacebuilding Commission and the initiatives supported by the Peacebuilding Fund. We emphasize the importance of providing sustainable financing, including strengthening partnerships with international and regional financial institutions and with the private sector. In this context, the GCC countries as a group have contributed over the past 5 years more than $14 billion US in global humanitarian and developmental assistance. These efforts have focused on qualitative initiatives that support sustainable peace. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the State of Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates rank 2nd, 3rd, and 5th among the top donor countries according to the OCHA Financial Tracking Service for 2025. The United Arab Emirates implements sustainable support programs through a number of charitable entities, including the Zayed Charity Institution, which works on addressing the root causes of conflicts and instability. The State of Kuwait, through the Kuwaiti Fund for Arab Economic Development, funds various projects that help address threats to global food insecurity. The Kingdom of Bahrain, through the Royal Humanitarian Foundation, provides a range of vital projects to support peace and its sustainability in the region. The Sultanate of Oman represents a model in the efforts exerted to achieve security and peace. In addition to extending assistance to affected populations through the Omani charitable organization, Oman is also a trusted mediator at both regional and international levels, and it has undertaken numerous efforts toward reconciliation among various parties. Madam President, the success of peacebuilding efforts requires integrating political development and humanitarian tracks in a way that delivers tangible results benefiting communities. It also necessitates strengthening the role of regional organizations, enhancing partnerships, empowering women and youth, and expanding collaboration with the civil society, therefore building more resilient societies capable of adapting to global changes. In conclusion, the GCC countries affirm that sustainable peace is based on partnership and prevention, on respecting state sovereignty, and on dialogue. It requires adherence to principles of tolerance and good neighborliness in a manner that supports security, stability, and development for all.

Thank you, President. I thank the distinguished representative of Bahrain, who was speaking on behalf of the Gulf Cooperation Council, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Croatia.

Thank you for convening this meeting. Croatia aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union, and I would like to underline a few points in my national capacity. We thank Germany for its leadership of the Peace Building Commission and welcome the strong results achieved in 2025. The Commission expanded its scope deepened partnership and strengthened its advisory role, holding 42 meetings across country, regional, and thematic areas. Country engagement was substantive. First-ever discussions on Haiti and renewed focus on Chad, Guinea-Bissau, and São Tomé and Príncipe showed responsiveness to evolving needs. The visit to Colombia reaffirmed international— reaffirmed international support for the final agreement. Regional engagement in Central Asia highlighted the value of dialogue and cooperation in preventing conflict. Partnerships advanced, especially with the African Union and international financial institutions, reinforcing the link between peacebuilding, sustaining peace, and development financing. Cross-cutting work also progressed with engagement of women and youth peacebuilders. These efforts deeply resonate with Croatia's own experience after the aggression against our country. A whole-of-society approach is essential in peacebuilding and sustaining peace efforts. Engaging women, youth, minorities, and vulnerable groups from the start is necessary for prevention. In this regard, Croatia has made the Women, Peace and Security Agenda a priority and is proud that women make up almost 15% of the personnel in Croatia's armed forces and 10% of those deployed in peace missions. Mine action is another critical area. After completing demining at home, Croatia now supports international efforts, including through its initiative She Demines, which promotes women's leadership in humanitarian demining. We commend the Peacebuilding Fund for its catalytic impact and longstanding support to prevention and peacebuilding, and wish it to continue to be nimble and flexible to produce the best peace dividends on the ground. Croatia is a contributor to the Fund and calls upon all to contribute. Looking ahead, we see three priorities for future PBC sessions. First, deepen follow-up mechanisms to track progress on prevention, elections, and transitional justice, with the Impact Hub playing a central role. Second, strengthen integration of financing discussions, translating needs into concrete national costed pathways. And third and final, expand joint analysis with regional organizations. With the successful review of the peacebuilding architecture, We are confident that the Commission will deliver even stronger support to nationally-led priorities. Croatia, as Vice-Chair, under Morocco's able leadership, remains committed to a more coherent, inclusive and effective Peacebuilding Commission. Finally, we thank the Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office for their dedicated support. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative Representative of Croatia, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

Mr. President, Excellencies, it's an honor to speak in this debate as we mark 20 years of the UN Peacebuilding architecture. We align ourselves with the statement of the European Union and would like to add the following remarks in our national capacity. We thank Morocco as current chair of the Peacebuilding Commission for its leadership and Germany for its chairmanship in 2025. We also thank the Assistant Secretary General Spehar and the Peacebuilding and Peace Support Office for the Peacebuilding Fund report and all of their very hard work. First, on the Peacebuilding Commission, the 2025 Peacebuilding Report shows a commission that's more active, more field-oriented, and more inclusive. It advises the Security Council, the General Assembly, and ECOSOC supports nationally-led prevention strategies and brings together the member states, international financial institutions, civil society, and local peacebuilders. This is the peacebuilding commission that we need. Secondly, on the peacebuilding fund and financing. The peacebuilding fund reports confirms the fund's catalytic role including emissions transitions and national prevention strategies. It also shows a gap between ambition and resources. Voluntary contributions have fallen to about $130 million a year, while demands and the $500 million target remain high. We welcome the start of assessed contributions as a more predictable— base. Yet voluntary funding, including from the Netherlands, must remain the backbone to keep the Fund flexible and responsive. Third, on peacebuilding and sustaining peace. The peacebuilding architecture review and the review of the peace operations send a clear message: our decisions in New York must have real impact on the ground. They must translate into mandates, guidance, and resources that link peace operations to long-term, nationally owned, and inclusive peacebuilding. For the Netherlands, peacebuilding must be nationally owned and inclusive. We welcome the Peacebuilding Commission's focus on longer-term political on accompaniments and strengthening institutions and on prevent— preventing relapse into conflict. We see scope for a more systematic role of the Peacebuilding Commission around mission settings. Mission mandates should be placed on the Peacebuilding Commission's agenda in a timely way so that its advice can shape establishment, renewal, and drawdown. The Peacebuilding Fund can then provide catalytic funding to support those nationally defined priorities. And finally, on partnerships. If we are serious about the peace continuum and sustaining peace, we must deepen cooperation with international financial institutions and regional organizations and invest in resident coordinators and peace development advisers so that all actors pull in the same direction. 20 years on, our task is to deliver on our promise that no country emerging from conflict is left to face its future alone. You can count on the Kingdom of the Netherlands as a committed partner in that effort. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representatives of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Portugal.

Madam President, at a time when conflicts are multiplying and peace feels fragile, One lesson is clear: peace must be built before, during, and after conflict. Peacebuilding is about prevention, but it is also about recovery, reconciliation, trust, institutions, and social cohesion. It helps societies emerge from conflict without falling back into violence. It is the difference between a fragile ceasefire and lasting peace, between an unsupported transition and one and that succeeds, between communities divided by war and communities able to rebuild together. This first Peacebuilding Week has given well-deserved visibility to these dimensions, and we thank the PBPSO for its outstanding work. As we mark the 20th anniversary of the Peacebuilding Fund, we should celebrate what it has achieved, but we should also be clear about what is at stake. The Fund is one of the UN's most practical tools for sustaining peace. It works where politics, security, human rights, and development meet. It supports nationally owned solutions. It gives space to local actors. It helps bridge the gap between immediate response and lasting peace. In 2025, the Fund supported 48 initiatives across 28 countries. It strengthened early warning systems. It supported the reintegration of displaced persons and former combatants. It helped communities resolve local conflicts. It advanced the participation of women and youth. And it backed national prevention and social cohesion strategies in line with the Pact for the Future. These are not technical results. They are peace dividends. They make communities safer. They strengthen institutions. They help countries— move from crisis management to sustainable peace. Portugal also commends the work of the Peacebuilding Commission. Its role is more relevant now than ever. It has broadened engagement, deepened partnerships and strengthened its advisory and bridging role with the Security Council and the General Assembly. This is the kind of bridge-building the United Nations needs more of. But ambition still runs ahead of resources. Demand for peacebuilding support is rising. Contributions are not keeping pace. The Fund cannot be expected to do more in more places with less. Predictable, adequate and sustainable financing is not a budgetary detail. It is a political choice. A choice to invest in prevention, to support transitions, to consolidate peace and to prevent hard-won gains from being lost. As a longstanding contributor to UN peace efforts and as a multi-year donor to the Fund, Portugal believes that peacekeeping, peacebuilding and sustaining peace are part of the same continuum. Looking ahead, peacebuilding must remain nationally owned, inclusive and people-centred. It must place women, youth and civil society at its core. And it must bring together Member States, regional organizations international financial institutions, the UN system, and local actors around the same purpose. As an incoming member of the Security Council, Portugal will work for a stronger peacebuilding architecture and advocate for a fund with the resources, flexibility, and political backing it needs. Because peace cannot be improvised after war. It must be prepared, accompanied, and sustained before during and after conflict. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Portugal, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Poland.

Madame President, first of all, I would like to thank you for convening this very important debate. Distinguished delegates, Poland fully aligns itself with the statements delivered by the European Union, but I would like to add some points on— in our national capacity. We welcome both the report of the Peacebuilding Commission on its 19th session and the report of the Secretary-General on the Peacebuilding Fund. As Vice Chair of the Peacebuilding Commission in 2025, Poland has seen firsthand how important peacebuilding has become in responding to today's complex challenges. Three key lessons stand out from our experience. First, preventing conflict is less costly and more effective than responding to crises after they occur. Second, national ownership is essential for lasting peace. Third, peacebuilding requires stable and predictable funding. The reports before us underscore a clear lesson: prevention is not only more effective but also far less costly than responding to conflict once it has taken hold. Evidence from across Africa, Latin America, and Asia consistently demonstrates that sustainable peace is built through inclusive governance, strong and accountable institutions, access to justice, economic opportunity, and social cohesion. Poland firmly believes that national ownership is the basis of successful peacebuilding. Sustainable peace cannot be imposed from the outside. International partners can support and facilitate, but lasting solutions must be led by national authorities and local communities.— we therefore welcome the increasing focus on national prevention strategies in the work of both the Commission and the Fund. In the same spirit, we welcome the growing participation of women and young people in peacebuilding processes. Madam Presidents, one issue deserves special attention. This is financing. The demand for peacebuilding support continues to grow. While available resources remain limited. And Poland considers operationalization of assessed contributions to the Peace Building Fund as an important step towards more predictable and sustainable financing. More discussion is needed on how to unlock the untapped potential of synergies between public and private investment in support of peace building activities. In this context, We welcome stronger cooperation between the UN, the World Bank, regional development banks, and other international financial institutions, because today's challenges require comprehensive approaches that combine political engagement, development expertise, and long-term financial support. Madam President, as the Peace Building Commission approaches its 20th anniversary, it is equally important to reflect on its future role. The Commission has demonstrated its value as a platform for dialogue, partnerships, and political support. Going forward, our focus should concentrate on increasing impact, strengthening accountability, and ensuring that successes are measured by concrete improvements in people's lives rather than by the number of meetings we organize. Ultimately, the credibility of the peacebuilding architecture will depend on its ability to deliver tangible results for people living in fragile and conflict-affected situations. I thank you, Madam President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Poland, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Colombia.

Thank you, Madam President. First of all, I would like to commend Morocco's leadership at the helm of the PBC this year. And I'd also like to thank Germany for their sterling work last year. The commemoration of 20 years of the UN peace-building architecture is an opportunity for us to take stock and to acknowledge that peace remains an urgent task. Since the end of World War II and the establishment of the United Nations, There has never been so many active state conflicts. Military expenditure continues to increase while resources for preventing conflicts and sustainable development are only decreasing. The climate crisis also continues to deepen the structural causes of violence. Against this backdrop, Peacebuilding and sustaining peace must be at the heart of our work. The role of the PBC as an advisory body, a bridge, and a forum for dialogue and a platform to mobilize financial support and to learn lessons is more necessary today than ever before. The Peacebuilding Fund, for its part, remains one of the main tools that we have at our disposal to support countries in their policies to sustain peace. We are concerned to see that there has been a reduction in voluntary contributions at a time when global needs continue to increase. Peace is never a lineal— a linear process, but rather it is a long-term task. And in Colombia, we have undergone this ourselves as a society with a clear belief that peace is only possible when the structural causes of violence are addressed. We value the support of the Commission, the Fund, and the international community for our national process. The Commission's visit to Colombia last year bore witness to this international commitment, and it was an opportunity for the Commission to hear directly from those who are building peace every day—communities, signatories of the agreement, victims, women, young people, and local authorities. This support has been critical in helping us to beef up our reinclusion policy. Today, more than 11,000 signatories are continuing their journey to civilian life with significant progress in terms of security, access to land, housing, and productive sustainability. The PBC's support has contributed to strengthen reinclusion projects with an environmental approach and with solutions for dignified housing. Our experience has shown that peace is built from the grassroots up, with the communities who have historically resisted violence, who have defended their lives in the midst of conflict, and who continue to commit to reconciliation, embracing differences and reaffirming their right to live in peace and with dignity. These communities will not cease in their determination to achieve a country in peace where dignity is a reality for for all. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Colombia, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan.

Madam President, in the past decade, the concept of peacebuilding has developed into a key integrating concept for the UN. While it has increasingly been recognized as a component of the peace and security pillar, it has also evolved an overarching perspective connecting all three pillars. As we mark the 20th anniversary of the peacebuilding architecture, its role in preventing conflict and sustaining peace is more important than ever. Today, addressing the increasing number of conflicts and their multifaceted root causes requires comprehensive and coherent approaches that take into account the perspective of human security. In this regard, we hope the peacebuilding architecture continues to play a pivotal role in ensuring that such an approach guides and integrates the efforts of the UN system towards sustaining peace. Building on the discussions and progress made over the past year, allow me to highlight the three points. First, It is essential to advance the implementation of the PBAR resolutions. At a time of increased fiscal constraints, Member States have rightly called for greater effectiveness and efficiency in delivering peacebuilding outcomes. This was precisely why the last year PBAR focused on the question of how the PBAR resolutions should serve as a concrete roadmap for enhancing impact. Their provisions must not remain merely aspirational. An important first step would be to identify practical action points where the commitments contained in the resolutions can be translated to intangible results on the ground. Second, we must continue to strengthen support for conflict prevention based on national ownership. Preventing conflict not only saves lives and— lives and protects hard-won development gains, but it is more cost-effective than responding after violence has erupted. We therefore welcome the growing number of countries presenting national prevention strategies in PBC meetings. This trend reflects the increasing recognition and demand among Member States for prevention efforts. The PVC can be a valuable platform for countries presenting national prevention strategies by helping to mobilize coherent, coordinated support from actions across and beyond the UN system. Such presentations would demonstrate national commitment and help clarify desired outcomes and priority actions, making it easier to monitor progress and identify areas where additional support may be needed. We encourage further utilization of the PVC in this manner and the PVC to strengthen follow-up on the implementation of these strategies. Third, it is critical for the PBF to maximize its role in building partnerships within and beyond the UN system. Its impact is greatest when it fosters broader partnerships so as to reduce the risk of relapse into conflict, sustain peace, and advance development. This should start within the UN system itself. In the transition from peacekeeping to peacebuilding, partnerships across the UN system are indispensable to avoid a financial cliff and preserve peacebuilding gains achieved during mission deployments. Building on this internal coherence, peacebuilding support must gradually shift to scalable and sustainable development efforts based on long-term partnership with IFIs and the private sector to further consolidate peace. Moving forward, it will be important to take stock of these catalytic approaches and partnership-building efforts that have proven most effective. From this perspective, the annual strategic dialogue between PBC and PBF, held for the first time last year, is an essential initiative —that should be continued. We would also encourage more frequent briefings by PVF recipient countries to the PBC on how PVF support has contributed to peacebuilding outcomes. Such exchanges would provide valuable lessons for all stakeholders.
To conclude, I refer I thank the distinguished representative of Japan, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil.

Madam President, I thank the former chair and the current chair of the PBC for presenting their reports and congratulate them for their wonderful work at the helm of the Commission. Let me start by commenting the SDGs report of the Peacebuilding Fund. The continued work of the PBF is a flexible and catalytic instrument in support of nationally owned peacebuilding and prevention efforts. In 2025, the Fund once again showed its added value by supporting initiatives in mission transition settings, cross-border and regional contexts, national prevention strategies, and women's and youth empowerment. In these areas, timely and relatively modest investments help sustain peace dividends, strengthen institutions, and prevent the outbreak of conflict. As Vice Chair of the PBC, Brazil encourages continued efforts to to strengthen coordination within the UN system, especially among the PBC, the PBF, the PBPSO, country teams, and resident coordinators. This helps ensure that the Fund's country-level investments are efficient, align with national priorities, and get political support from the PBC. But ambition must be matched by— with resources. We welcome the first use of assessed contributions to the Fund. This allows more predictable and sustainable financing. Despite the current financial constraints, the assessed contributions must be fully disbursed and projects funded by them must be showcased to the general membership. The PBC did a great job during its 19th session. It has continued to strengthen its advisory, leveraging, and convening roles.— it has broadened its geographical scope and deepened partnerships with regional organizations, IFIs, and civil society. PBC's support for national priorities enables it to serve as a political platform for States to share best practices and lessons learned in prevention and peacebuilding. The reports on the PBC and PBF The activities are clear. The PBC and the PBF are strongest if they work in synergy. The PBC provides political support, visibility, and partner mobilization. The Fund provides catalytic resources to help translate nationally defined priorities into concrete results on the ground, which should be seen as pilots for new projects. Madam President, Brazil fully supports the implementation of the 2025 UN Peacebuilding Architecture Review. We reaffirm our commitment to inclusive and impactful peacebuilding. Supporting Member States in preventing conflict and achieving sustainable peace is at the heart of the UN's job. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Brazil. Before proceeding further, members are informed that at 12:30 the joint debate will be suspended for the Assembly to proceed to the consideration of the other items announced in the journal for this meeting. In view of the significantly higher number of inscriptions for this debate than in the previous session, the remaining speakers will be heard at a later date to be announced. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Guatemala.

Señora Presidenta, Madam President, Guatemala is grateful for the presentation of the annual report of the PPC and the Secretary-General's report on the Peacebuilding Fund. Both documents reflect the increasing request for support from the two bodies and the need to strengthen financing mechanisms and mechanisms for cooperation that make it possible to respond to these challenges. We also recognize the role of the Commission as a forum for dialogue and advice that contributes to strengthening consistency among international efforts and to promote viable solutions for countries. Guatemala agrees with the focus on national ownership, prevention, and inclusion as fundamental pillars for building lasting peace. Madam President, for Guatemala, peacebuilding means strengthening trust between institutions and citizens, broadening fora for participation, promoting dialogue, and building peaceful mechanisms for transition post-conflicts. We welcome the support that the Fund has provided to national efforts geared towards beefing up the rule of law, social cohesion, and preventing conflicts. Guatemala's experience shows that the most sustainable solutions are those that are built from the ground up with the broad participation of communities and with strong national leadership. That is why we highlight the progress that has been made in promoting dialogue between states and indigenous communities and indigenous— and initiatives to strengthen the participation of women and youth in peacebuilding. We also stress the importance of strengthening national prevention strategies. Investing in prevention doesn't just reduce human and economic costs, it also contributes to establishing propitious conditions for sustainable development and social cohesion in general. Madam President, Guatemala believes it is critical to continue strengthening the Peace Building Fund and to ensure predictable flexible and sustainable resources that will make it possible to respond to increasing demands for support, prevention, and peacebuilding. Lastly, we reiterate our commitment to the peacebuilding and sustaining peace agenda and to strengthening a peacebuilding architecture that is human-centered, based on inclusion, dialogue, and national ownership. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Guatemala, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nepal.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. First of all, I thank you, Madam President, for convening this timely debate as we mark the 20th anniversary of the United Nations peacebuilding architecture. At a time when we witness a growing number of conflicts around the world, the imperative of peacebuilding has become more evident than ever. Peacebuilding is not only about preventing the recurrence of conflicts, but also about building resilient societies by investing in people, in trust, and in the institutions that bind communities together. It is about fostering social cohesion and advancing sustainable development. Madam President, let me highlight a few points. First, based on Nepal's experience, a nationally-led and nationally-owned peace process is indispensable. In this context, we welcome the stronger focus on voluntary national war prevention and peacebuilding strategies. Including the Peacebuilding Commission's efforts to bolster social cohesion and national capacities to manage conflict risk. Second, peacebuilding must be prevention-warranted and people-centered. The meaningful participation of women, youth, and civil societies is indispensable. They must not be seen as beneficiaries, but as co-architects of peace. Their perspectives and their leadership strengthen legitimacy, deepen reconciliation, and ensure that peace endures. Third, we must deepen coherence and complementarity across the United Nations systems. Stronger partnerships with international financial institutions, regional and sub-regional bodies, and civil society can unlock expertise and innovations. Similarly, South-South and triangular cooperation remain essential channels for shared learning and capacity building. Fourth, Adequate, predictable, and sustained financing is essential. Nepal supports innovative financing mechanisms and deeper engagements with international financial institutions. We also value the Peace Building Fund's catalytic role in advancing nationally-owned prevention and peacebuilding and in helping countries address risks before they escalate. Fifth, the United Nations must enhance its preventive diplomacy, early warning, and mediation capacities. Prevention is not only morally right, it is cost-effective and it is politically wise. Finally, Madam President, greater emphasis is needed on addressing the structural drivers of conflict. Among those is poverty, exclusions, inequality, and lack of opportunities. Effective implementations of the 2030 Agenda must be accelerated as a strategic investment in prevention, in peacebuilding, in sustaining peace. To conclude, Madam President, peacebuilding is our shared and moral imperatives. Let us reaffirm our commitment to ensure that every society can live in dignity, in security, and in opportunity. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nepal I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Madam President, Excellencies, allow me to extend Indonesia's appreciation to the Secretary-General and the Peacebuilding Commission for their reports. These reports are timely when we face both rising demand for peacebuilding and heightened expectations for prevention. Sustaining peace is not a one-time program but a long-term investment in people and institutions. In this context, Indonesia would like to share 5 points. First, the alignment of the Commission's work with the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review must be preserved. Stronger system-wide coherence ensures effectiveness and efficiency. National ownership guarantees sustainable and impactful implementations for communities the architecture is meant to serve. Second, there is more opportunity for the Commission's growing advisory roles, as reflected in its engagement with the Security Council, the General Assembly, and the Economic and Social Council.. We encourage this engagement to deepen, particularly on mission transitions, prevention, and sustaining peace. Third, we value the catalytic results of the Peacebuilding Fund, which continue to deliver meaningful peacebuilding outcomes across diverse contexts. We attach great importance to the Fund's sustained investment in inclusion initiatives, support for national prevention strategies and women and youth empowerment. Fourth, innovative financing is the key to address the current gap of resources in the Fund. Partnerships with international financial institutions, regional development banks, and private sectors will help the Fund match its ambitions with delivery. Fifth, we value the deepening synergies between the Commission and the Fund., including their first annual Strategic Dialogue. These synergies can extend further through stronger Commission bridging with regional organizations and through sustained engagement with civil society and local peacebuilders. Madam President, Indonesia's engagement with the Commission and with the Peacebuilding Fund spans the full two decades of their existence. Through our peacekeeping personnel, Through our active partnerships with the Fund and through our South-South and triangular cooperation efforts, we have consistently supported people-centered peacebuilding, and we will continue to do so. Indonesia reaffirms its full support for the implementation of the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review and for the broader missions this Commission carries forward. I thank you, Madam President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovenia.

Madam President, distinguished colleagues, as we mark 20 years of the UN Peacebuilding Commission and of the Peacebuilding Fund, the inaugural UN Peacebuilding Week is both a celebration and a call for action. The week provides an annual platform for inclusive dialogues and greater visibility of peacebuilding. It enables a continuous focus on peacebuilding in times of increasing challenges for peace. Slovenia trusts that today's UN General Assembly session contributes to this end. Slovenia had the honor and privilege to co-facilitate, together with Egypt, the PIBR Twin Resolutions, with a clear objective to make peacebuilding more impactful on the ground, where it matters most. The unanimous adoption of these resolutions at a time of growing geopolitical divisions and financial strain was an encouraging signal of unity and collective responsibility for prevention and peacebuilding. It was a demonstration of trust of the Member States in peacebuilding and the role of the UN in it. We must continue to build on this momentum, demonstrated also through so many events organized on peacebuilding this week. And this is why I come to the General Assembly today with three messages. The first message is a call for action. PBAR calls for a stronger prevention lens, with peacebuilding clearly anchored in inclusive national ownership. It asks for greater system-wide coherence across peace and security, development and human rights. It invites us to develop more effective partnerships with regional and financial actors. The second message is a reminder. A reminder to the UN General Assembly to make use of the UN Peacebuilding Commission for strategic and context-specific advice, as well as to convene joint debates or other forms of interactive exchanges. The PPC advice for the General Assembly on the causes of conflict and promotion of durable peace and sustainable development in Africa from May this year is a good example. And the third message is an invitation. An invitation to the Member States to consider even closer collaboration with BBC, to use it as a platform to seek support and advice while fostering inclusive national ownership as a foundation of sustainable peace, to promote, develop and implement prevention and peacebuilding strategies, to share good practices and lessons learned. Madam President, in the past 3 years, here in New York, I sat through countless briefings on protracted conflicts and post-conflict contexts around the world. I listened to reports filled with numbers— with numbers, persons displaced, schools demolished, health systems collapsed, trust eroded. But what stayed with me are the stories of peacebuilders. It is the stories of communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Colombia, and Syria where young peacebuilders work side by side to rebuild trust after years of conflict. It is the stories of grassroots women peacebuilders in Central African Republic, Mauritania or Liberia who continue to mediate local disputes long after international attention has moved elsewhere. These stories remind me that conflict is not inevitable, but neither is The goal is peace. Peace must be built patiently, inclusively, constantly. I am truly glad that the UN Peacebuilding Week offered a chance for us to hear these stories and see their results. No effort invested in prevention is too much and no investment in peacebuilding is too costly. The real cost is paid when we fail. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovenia, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Thailand.

Madam President, Thailand thanks you for convening this important meeting and is honored to share its perspectives on peacebuilding at this landmark inaugural Peacebuilding Week, an essential outcome of the 2025 Review of the UN Peacebuilding Architecture as follows. First, prevention is the most effective strategy for conflict resolution. Thailand welcomes the Peacebuilding Commission's increased focus on supporting voluntary, nationally-owned prevention strategies in line with the Pact for the Future. We believe that investing in early warning and rapid response, including community-based monitoring, is far more effective than reacting after conflict occurs. Second, to succeed in sustaining peace, we must address root causes and drivers of conflict through a human-centered approach. Peace, development, and human security are interlinked and mutually reinforcing. Ownership is key. We must move beyond mere participation to ensuring that women and youth are central to the governance of peace processes. Thailand applauds the PBC for reaching a 63% participation rate for women peacebuilders in its meetings this year. Third, effective peacebuilding requires strong coordination and partnership. Thailand supports the Commission's unique bridging role in connecting the Security Council, the General Assembly, and ECOSOC to ensure system-wide coherence. We encourage the PBC to further expand its engagement with regional organizations such as ASEAN to exchange best practices on cross-regional responses to transnational threats. Fourth, peacebuilding requires adequate, predictable, and sustained financing. While global demand for conflict prevention is growing, voluntary contributions have declined significantly from $180 million in 2020 to $132.3 million in 2025. Thailand welcomes the historic first utilization of assessed contributions for the Peace Building Fund in 2025 to stabilize its operations. We also encourage innovative financing and public-private partnerships to bolster the Fund's catalytic role in unlocking larger-scale investments from international financial institutions. Madam President, Thailand appreciates the comprehensive reporting of the PBC and the impact-driven results of the PBF, which has demonstrated success with up to an 80% reduction in conflicts in specific intervention areas. Thailand remains committed to strengthening the UN peacebuilding architecture to ensure that it remains flexible, accountable, and impactful. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Thailand, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ireland.

Ireland aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union. Adoption of the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review demonstrated that meaningful outcomes through multilateral cooperation remain possible, even in the most challenging of times. We must now ensure that we translate our shared commitments into action. This requires renewed focus and ambition on prevention. Investing in prevention remains one of the most effective ways to reduce human suffering, protect development gains, and build lasting stability. Yet prevention efforts remain underprioritised and underfunded. We must invest more consistently in addressing the root causes of conflict. Specifically, Ireland believes that human rights are not simply an outcome of peacebuilding, they are one of its core foundations. Respect for human rights, equality, and access to justice help address grievances before they escalate into violence, and strong accountability processes can guard against reoccurrence. Our own experience on the island of Ireland taught us that peace is a process, not a singular event. Peacebuilding is rarely linear. Progress can be fragile, setbacks can occur, and sustaining peace requires patience, persistence, and political courage above all else. Durable peace cannot be imposed or secured through addressing short-term considerations alone. To build lasting peace, inclusive political solutions and a commitment to addressing the underlying drivers of conflict are essential. In this regard, we underscore the importance of UN mediation. The UN brings unique legitimacy and convening power to peace processes, and UN envoys can play an essential role, including to build trust between parties. We must continue to support and invest in these capacities. We must also recognize the growing impact of climate change on stability and security, and relatedly, the contribution that climate action can make to sustaining peace. President, earlier this week Ireland was pleased to organize an event on strengthening the peacebuilding-peace operations nexus. That discussion reinforced the contribution that UN peace operations make to conflict prevention, local conflict resolution, and peacebuilding. We encourage the Security Council to consistently support the integration of peacebuilding during mission mandate cycles, including during mission transitions. Ireland reiterates its strong support for the Peace Building Fund. At a time when resources are under increasing pressure, sustained and predictable funding for peace building is more important than ever. Finally, peace building must be inclusive and locally owned. Women, young people, civil society, local peace builders and minority groups must have a meaningful role in shaping the decisions that affect their very futures. This is essential because local voices and communities are at the heart of all successful peacebuilding efforts. Our collective responsibility is to ensure that their efforts are supported with patience, with resources, and with political commitment. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ireland, and I now give the floor I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Egypt.

Madam President, our debate today is of particular significance as we discuss the first two reports on the PBC and the PBF after the adoption of the outcomes of the review of the peacebuilding architecture of 2025. And as part of the inaugural Peacebuilding Week, the outcome represented a milestone to strengthen the efficiency of the UN peacebuilding architecture. This debate is also of particular significance because it comes on the sidelines of the inaugural Peacebuilding Week, embodying state commitment to translate the review outcomes into political momentum, practical dialogue, and an annual inclusive platform to support the peacebuilding agenda at the United Nations. Egypt commends the efforts of the PBC and the PBF during the reporting period. We welcome the report's growing consensus on the importance of investing in prevention and peacebuilding as the most cost-effective strategic option that is by far less costly than managing conflicts after their outbreak. We also welcome the growing focus on national ownership, social cohesion, and building national institutions that can manage conflict risks and address the root causes. The two reports confirmed important findings that align with our Egyptian and African vision. This includes the need to transition from short-term approaches to building sustainable national capacities. This also includes increasing the interlinkage between peace, development, and human rights, and expanding partnership with regional and international financial institutions. This also includes supporting national prevention and peacebuilding strategies at the most effective framework to achieve tangible and lasting results on the ground. In this context, Egypt believes that strengthening the advisory convening and bridging role of the PBC is a top priority for the period to come. We underscore the importance of strengthening synergies between the PBC and the PBF. Resources must be geared towards national priorities set by countries themselves. This will strengthen the impact of UN interventions and ensure their sustainability. Egypt also underscores the importance of providing adequate, predictable, and sustained funding— financing for the PBF. We must maintain catalytic financing in support of national priorities.. We call on all countries to pay their assessed contributions to the PBF. In Africa— regarding Africa, we commend the report's focus on the importance of partnership between the UN and the African Union, including through the ongoing institutional dialogue between the PBC and the AU Peace and Security Council. Madam President, we will pursue our effective role in supporting the peacebuilding agenda at the United Nations. We have co-facilitated jointly with Slovenia, the Peacebuilding Architecture Review of 2025. We concluded this review process. We also coordinated the program on the side events of the inaugural Peacebuilding Week jointly with Slovenia. And this inaugural Peacebuilding Week has been successful to date. In conclusion, we look forward to building on the outcomes of the 2025 review to ensure that the UN peacebuilding system is more effective, more impactful, and more responsive to the needs of countries and peoples. Thank you, Madam President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Egypt. Aishkurou. I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, I am grateful for this opportunity to address the General Assembly on peacebuilding and sustaining peace and to reflect on the important work of the Peacebuilding Commission and the Peacebuilding Fund. I will make 3 brief points. First, on prevention. Both reports highlight a clear shift towards prevention that is nationally led, inclusive, and grounded in local realities. This should remain at the heart of our work.

The BBC has consistently emphasized national ownership as a guiding principle. At the same time, the PBF has expanded its support to nationally owned prevention strategies.

Helping countries to address root causes of conflict. This reflects a growing consensus: Sustainable peace cannot be imposed, it must be nurtured.

Our role is to support countries to act earlier and more effectively to prevent conflict, including through targeted and evidence-based approaches.

Second, on system-wide coherence, the PBC continues to demonstrate its value as a convening platform, bringing together member states, the UN system, and partners around coherent responses to conflict risks. At country level, Resident Coordinators play a critical role in ensuring that peacebuilding, development, and humanitarian efforts are aligned behind nationally-led priorities. Strengthening coherence between these actors is essential if we are to address the complex and interconnected drivers of conflict and deliver real impact on the ground.

And third, on partnerships. Impactful peacebuilding requires stronger and more diverse partnerships.

The PBC and PBF have both made important progress in this regard, recognizing that these actors bring complementary strengths.

Financial institutions provide scale and long-term investment, while civil society brings local access, knowledge, and legitimacy. These partnerships are not just complementary, they are essential.

Continuously strengthening these partnerships is critical to ensuring that peacebuilding efforts are effective, inclusive, and sustainable. Excellencies, the 2025 review of the peacebuilding architecture provided a timely opportunity to build on UN peacebuilding's achievements over the last 20 years. We must now translate commitments into action by investing in prevention, strengthening coherence, and deepening partnerships. The UK remains committed to working with all partners to deliver on this agenda. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of France.

Madame la Présidente. Madame President, I'd like to thank you for convening this debate. We commend the work of Germany and Morocco as they presided over the PBC over the last 2 years.

Thank you also to the vice chairs.

I'd like to underscore 3 points. First, the Peacebuilding Commission has an important role to to play in promoting sustained political commitments towards peace efforts. Last year, it showed this in Colombia, where it went to demonstrate the international support for the implementation of the 2016 peace accords; in Liberia, where it highlighted the participation of women in the peace process; in Haiti, where the PBC supported the electoral process and helped to prevent armed violence. The Commission's commitment attests to the fact that it's important to ensure peacekeeping, peacebuilding, and prevention are all integrated so as to ensure comprehensive peace. Second, we support the Peacebuilding Fund as it invests in prevention and post-conflict processes. It is uniquely positioned to catalyze funding and work with all actors on the ground, as well as the private sector and international financial institutions. The PBF works in transition contexts. It has, for instance, helped MONUSCO to withdraw from Tanganyika and other areas. Climate, peace, and security is something that's been focused in the Pacific, helping Kiribati, Tuvalu, and other states. France is proud to be one of the main contributors to the PBF. It's vital that we continue to support this tool, in particular by mobilizing funding mechanisms that are innovative, as well as by ensuring there are new donors who join our ranks. Third, the Peacebuilding Architecture Review, PBA, highlighted the need to prioritize the need for concrete outcomes, concrete results. This should help us to galvanize the work of the PBC and the PBF in areas where they have the most— produced the most value added, the greatest catalyst effect. Concretely contributing to putting an end to conflicts. Prioritizing this commitment, as well as the visibility of the effects, is how peacebuilding can help contribute to sustaining peace. France stands ready and determined to play its role in this process. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of France, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of India.

Madam President, we appreciate the convening of today's debate on peacebuilding and sustaining peace, which coincides with the first Peacebuilding Week of the United Nations. Let me begin by recognizing the good work of my brother, Ambassador Omar Hilali, the chair of the Peacebuilding Commission. Of Germany and Ambassadors Anja and Rickleff, the previous chair, other Bureau members, as also Egypt and Slovenia, for their co-facilitating role for the fourth review of the peacebuilding architecture review. Madam President, we note that significant progress was made during the 19th session of the Commission, including the fourth review of the peacebuilding architecture, the presentation of the first national peacebuilding strategy— and the first annual Strategic Dialogue with the Peacebuilding Fund following the General Assembly's approval of a $50 million assessed contribution to the Fund. The Secretary-General's report on the Peacebuilding Fund notes a decline in voluntary contributions over the past 3 years. At the same time, the organization's ongoing liquidity situation has constrained the availability of assessed contributions for peacebuilding activities. This is a concerning pattern. To ensure greater impact with reduced resources. Resource prioritization should be directed to post-conflict settings. We would like to see further progress on this front during the development of the Fund's next strategy. Madam President, the theme of the Peacebuilding Week of UN Peacebuilding at 20, Partnerships for Innovation, Inclusion and Impact, is very timely. Earlier this year, we organized a retreat on peacekeeping and peacebuilding in an evolving global context in partnership with all stakeholders. We recognize the importance of fostering trust-based partnerships to advance peacebuilding and sustain peace. Such partnerships can be built provided national ownership remains a central principle across all peacebuilding activities. Moreover, peacebuilding must move beyond the traditional donor-recipient approach. It should be demand-driven, reflecting the needs and priorities of national governments, with the international community playing a supportive role by providing financial and technical assistance. Additionally, peacebuilding should prioritize building institutional resilience and national capacity in post-conflict settings. Madam President, earlier this month, India's Major Abhilasha Barak was named the 2025 Military Gender Advocate of the Year. It reaffirms our commitment to the Women, Peace and Security Agenda, especially in peacebuilding. We stand ready to work with all partners on peacebuilding and to share our unique experience in nation-building.

I thank you, Madam President.
I thank the distinguished representative of India, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Rwanda.

Madam President, thank you very much for giving Rwanda the floor. First, we commend the Peacebuilding Commission for its continued contribution to advancing peacebuilding and sustaining peace. Today, we meet at a time when conflict is becoming more complex, more prolonged, and more costly. Across the world, wars, political instability, are growing—

and are growing inequalities are reversing development gains and placing millions of lives at risk. Yet the two reports before us offer hope.

The two reports remind us that peacebuilding works, not in theory, not on paper, but in communities and in people's lives. The evidence presented is comparing across different regions investments in prevention, dialogue, local ownership, and social cohesion have helped reduce violence, strengthen trust, and build more resilient societies. This should not surprise all of us. Peace is rarely secured by force alone. It is sustained when institutions function, when communities feel included, when grievances are addressed, and when people have confidence in their future.

Madam President, one figure should give us all a pause.

The world spends approximately $2.7 trillion on military expenditure, the highest ever recorded.

Yet we continue to struggle to mobilize a fraction of that amount for prevention and peacebuilding.

The reports before us remind us that peacebuilding is not a cost, it is an investment. Every conflict prevented, every community reconciled leads to a huge investment. The question, therefore, is not whether we can afford to invest in peacebuilding, but whether we can afford not to to do so. Mr. President, Madam President, this is why Rwanda welcomes the outcome of the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture and its strong emphasis on prevention, national ownership, inclusivity, and greater coherence across all the UN system. We welcome the continued impact of the Peacebuilding Fund, and which— it shows that the Fund is doing great work in all communities it is investing its resources. We must invest earlier, act more coherently, and strengthen support for nationally owned peacebuilding efforts. And in a world facing growing uncertainty, it remains one of the wisest investments the international community can make. For Rwanda, that investment transformed our nation Therefore, the reports before us demonstrate that it can do the same elsewhere. I thank you very much, Mr. President.
Madam President, I thank the distinguished representative of Rwanda, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of South Africa.

Thank you very much, Madam President. South Africa is honored to deliver its national statement to this august assembly under the theme "Peacebuilding and Sustaining Peace." We thank Germany for the report of the PBC on its 19th session. At the same time, we welcome the 2025 report of the Secretary-General on the Peacebuilding Fund. We also take this opportunity to express our gratitude to Morocco, the current Chair of the PBC. Madam President, while the report highlights the Commission's relevance, demonstrating growing value in convening diverse partners, advising UN organs, and supporting nationally-led priorities,, including more systematic engagement on cross-border risks, transitions, and prevention. It also notes persistent gaps in financing and operations. Financing for peacebuilding remains unpredictable and insufficient. UN support at the country level is uneven, despite commitments made through the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review. Partnerships with regional organizations, especially the African Union, require deeper operational alignment to reflect their central role in sustaining peace on the continent. The 2025 report of the Secretary-General on the Peace Building Fund reinforces this message. The PBF continues to demonstrate impact through rapid deployment, catalytic support, and strong results in prevention and transitions. South Africa therefore reiterates an unequivocal call. Peacebuilding must be financed at a scale that matches the risks we face. Voluntary contributions alone are insufficient. We should consider innovative financing options and deepen partnerships with international financial institutions to secure predictable, sustained support. Madam President, as we look ahead, South Africa reaffirms its commitment to ensuring that The peacebuilding architecture remains fit for purpose. We support the PBC's forward-looking agenda, which emphasizes national ownership and the interlinkages between peace, development, security, and human rights as we mark the Commission's 20th anniversary. National ownership must remain the foundation of all peacebuilding efforts. Coherent, integrated UN support must be delivered consistently at the country level. Regional organizations, particularly the AU, must be engaged as strategic partners whose leadership is fully recognized. We welcome the PBC's efforts to assist member states in strengthening prevention capacities and developing peacebuilding strategies aligned with national priorities. Equally, peacebuilding financing must be predictable, adequate, and sustained, including for the PBF. South Africa therefore stresses that inclusive peacebuilding must guide our collective efforts, with women, youth, and affected communities meaningfully shaping the solutions that define their future. We appreciate the PBC's commitment to gender and youth strategies and its efforts to strengthen system-wide coherence with the Peacebuilding Fund. Madam President, It is vital for the PBC to enhance its visibility, to advocate more effectively for the political commitment and resources required for peacebuilding. We welcome efforts to increase the visibility of open meetings, including high-level events and press releases, the development of a communication strategy with the Department of Global Communications, and expanded engagement across digital platforms to promote peacebuilding initiatives. Madam President, South Africa's own history teaches us that peace is built through dialogue, justice, and inclusive development, not through fragmented interventions or short-term crisis response. The PBC and PBF remain essential instruments for advancing these principles, but they require our political— our collective political will. We therefore urge member states to match their rhetoric with action. The cost of inaction is instability, humanitarian crisis, and the erosion of development gains. The cost of prevention is far lower and the dividends thereof are far greater. South Africa stands ready to work with all partners to advance a peaceful, just, and inclusive world. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of South Africa, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea.

Madam President, for Republic of Korea, sustaining peace is not a concept learned from palace paper. Rather, it is reality written into our national experience and development trajectory. We know both the devastation of conflict and the power of sustained peace. It is perhaps no coincidence that a decade ago the United Nations advanced a simple but potent idea: preventing conflict is more effective than responding to it. Today, as violent conflicts surge to their highest levels since the Second World War and resources become increasingly strained, peacebuilding cannot simply become larger in scale. Instead, it must become smarter and more nimble. Allow me to highlight the following 3 reflections. First, we must prioritize prevention at the heart of peacebuilding by addressing risk early and empowering societies to stay on a peace-positive path. Peacebuilding's comparative Our strategy lies in deftly addressing political risks and tensions, which are often beyond the reach of mere development or humanitarian assistance. By supporting dialogue, boosting inclusion, and enhancing national capacity for prevention, it can help reduce conflict risk before they escalate. We therefore Welcome expanding efforts to translate the concept of prevention into concrete national strategies and institutions, as demonstrated by experiences such as Mauritania and Papua New Guinea. Second, we must strengthen impact, accountability, and learning. Peacebuilding often operates in uncertain political special environments where some degree of risk tolerance is essential. Yet risk tolerance does not mean being indifferent to results. We need a stronger culture of learning what works, what does not, and why. Approaches such as the Peacebuilding Impact Hub can help reinforce evidence-based approaches across the peace— peacebuilding peacebuilding system. Third, the current peacebuilding financing gap is also a partnership gap. As demands continue to grow and resources continue to contract, stronger partnership and clearer prioritization will be essential moving forward. The peacebuilding fund should most remain a catalytic, flexible, and timely instrument, while leveraging partnerships across the broader peacebuilding ecosystem to maximize impact. These principles should be reflected in the POND's next strategy. As host of this year's PBF Strategic Dialogue, the Republic of Korea looks forward to working with partners to advance these important discussions. Madam President, as we now move from last year's review of the peace-building architecture to today's implementation, our focus should be clear: delivering a more preventive, more connected, and more effective peace-building architecture. The Republic of Korea stands ready to actively contribute to this vital effort.
I thank you. I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Madam President.

As a strong supporter of peacebuilding, Pakistan welcomes the convening of this important debate and the Peacebuilding Week. I also thank Ambassadors Beattain and Hilal, the former and current chairs of the Peacebuilding Commission, for their briefings. Madam President, 20 years since the establishment of UN peacebuilding architecture, it is opportune to reflect on the achievements, challenges, and lessons learned, and also to reaffirm our collective commitment to this endeavor in an increasingly complex global environment. Two decades ago, when PBC was established, there were relatively fewer conflicts. Peacekeeping was more effectively utilized in many theaters, helping countries emerge from conflict, and that brought focus on how to consolidate peace and prevent relapse so that the hard-won gains are not lost. It seems that now there is less peace to keep and lesser even to build, and there is a scramble for resources that are becoming scarce. We must therefore assess the whole situation seriously and holistically to deliver the promise of peacebuilding. As other colleagues have noted, peace is not an event. It is a continuum from conflict prevention to peacemaking and peacekeeping to post-conflict recovery and peacebuilding, and that are often interconnected and mutually reinforcing. Particularly in intrastate or complex crises, sustainable peace can best be achieved when people begin to experience tangible peace dividends through improved governance, stronger institutions, social inclusion, and economic opportunity for a better future. Experience has shown that that peacekeeping alone would not secure lasting peace. On the other hand, peacebuilding cannot be delayed till after the peacekeepers have left. It must be integrated from the outset. And this transition from peacekeeping to peacebuilding and ultimately to nationally-led development requires sustained political commitment, adequate resources, and coherent support from the international community. In this regard, Pakistan welcomes the outcomes of the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review facilitated by Egypt and Slovenia. The emphasis on national ownership, stronger links between Peacebuilding Commission and the principal organs of the United Nations, enhanced follow-up, and improved coherence across the UN system, including with the IFIs, reflects priorities that we have consistently supported. We commend the growing role of the Commission, particularly its country-specific configurations, as a platform for dialogue, partnership building, and resource mobilization. Pakistan further recognizes the important contribution of the Peace Building Fund, Experiences shared by countries with UN peacebuilding programs illustrate the practical difference that timely and flexible peacebuilding support can make on ground. Sustained support for peacebuilding financing therefore remains essential. As one of the largest troop-contributing countries to UN peacekeeping operations and a founding member of the Peacebuilding Commission Pakistan has witnessed firsthand the importance of linking security gains with institution-building, reconciliation, and socio-economic recovery. After all, it was this inextricable link between peace and development, and the need for a comprehensive approach addressing the root causes, that led to the establishment of the Commission and the Fund. We must therefore remain focused on that central purpose: helping countries prevent conflict, sustain peace, and avoid relapse. Pakistan will continue working with all member states to advance this shared objective. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Pakistan, I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Angola.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, as we commemorate the 20th anniversary of peacebuilding architecture, and celebrate the first-ever Peacebuilding Week, this annual session offers an important opportunity to reflect on lessons learned, strengthen partnership, advance more effective approaches to sustaining peace. Angola's experience demonstrates that peacebuilding is a long-term national endeavor, founded on national ownership, inclusive dialogue, and sustained partnership. Following almost three decades of conflict, peace was consolidated through the joint efforts of national institutions, local communities, regional organizations, the United Nations, and international partners. This partnership supported reconstruction, institutional building, and national reconciliation, creating foundations for sustainable peace and development. One example of United Nations support that has proven particularly impactful most helpful has been its sustained assistance in strengthening national capacities for peacebuilding, institutional building, and reconciliation. Our experience confirms that international support delivers lasting results when it reinforces nationally identified priorities, promotes inclusion, and remains engaged beyond the immediate post-conflict phase. Investing Investing in peacebuilding is both a strategic and cost-effective investment. It strengthens institutions, fosters social cohesion, and reduces the risk of conflict recurrence. By contrast, failing to sustain peacebuilding efforts carries far greater costs, including renewed violence, humanitarian crises, displacement, and the erosion of development gains.. The implementation of the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review Resolution should therefore deliver one essential change: a more coherent, integrated, and adequately financed United Nations approach at the country level, bringing together peacebuilding, development, humanitarian, and financial actors in support of national-owned priorities, including through a Strengthen Peacebuilding Fund Strategy for 2027-2030. Mr. President, national reconciliation remains at the heart of Angola's peacebuilding efforts. The Commission for Reconciliation in Memory of the Victims of Political Conflicts between 1975 and 2002 is promoting healing by locating identifying and returning the remains of victims to their families for dignified burial while preserving historical memory and strengthening reconciliation and national cohesion. This experience demonstrates that addressing the legacy of conflict with dignity, compassion and inclusiveness is indispensable to preventing future divisions and sustaining peace. Looking ahead to 2030, Angola is committed to strengthening preventive diplomacy, promoting inclusive national dialogue, and sharing its peacebuilding experience with the countries emerging from conflict. We will continue to advocate for stronger partnerships that place national ownership at the centre and translate political commitments into lasting peace dividends for communities. I thank you.

Thank you, Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. I have the honor to introduce on behalf of Bahrain Singapore, and my own country, Tajikistan, draft Resolution A/80/L54 entitled International Decade of Strengthening of Peace for Future Generations 2027-2036. This initiative was proposed by the President of the Republic of Tajikistan, His Excellency Emmanuelle Ramon at the General Assembly of the 79th Session of the General Assembly.

It reflects a commitment to strengthening peace as a shared and forward-looking responsibility towards present and future generations. Madam President, the draft resolution is grounded in the purposes and principles of the UN Charter. It reaffirms the obligation to settle disputes by peaceful means, and to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.

It also draws upon the Declaration and Programme of Action on the—

on a Culture of Peace, as well as the commitment contained in the Pact of the Future and the Declaration on Future Generations adopted at the Summit of the Future in September 2024. By this draft resolution, the General Assembly would proclaim the period 2027-2036 as the International Decade of Strengthening of Peace for Future Generations. The objectives of the decade are to promote peace, encourage dialogue and reconciliation, and strengthen intergenerational engagement, including with and among children, youth, and older persons. With a view to ensuring that the perspectives and needs of future generations are reflected in relevant policies and decision-making processes. The draft resolution invites Member States, UN system, regional organizations, civil society, academia, and other relevant stakeholders to contribute to the observance of the decade through voluntary and nationally driven activities, which may include policy dialogues, educational programmes, awareness-raising initiatives and exchanges of best practices.

Madam President, the resolution also recognizes the valuable contribution of Member States, leaders and peoples who have promoted peace, dialogue, reconciliation and national unity.

Through inclusive processes, confidence-building measures, post-conflict recovery, and long-term investment in social cohesion.

Such experiences provide important lessons for building resilient and cohesive societies.

In this regard, it's important to note that the recent positive development— developments in Central Asia, where countries of the region including Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and my own country, Tajikistan, have addressed longstanding border issues through constructive dialogue and peaceful means by signing Khujand Declaration. This achievement demonstrates that political will, mutual respect, and diplomacy can deliver lasting solutions and strengthen regional stability. Madam President, We have engaged in open and transparent consultations with member states throughout this process and are encouraged by the broad support the initiative has received. Therefore, we would like to sincerely thank all delegations for their constructive engagement and support during the process.

Tajikistan expresses sincere appreciation also to all delegations that they have joined as co-sponsors and invites those that have not yet done so to consider extending their support prior to the adoption of the resolution.

Madam President, we look forward to the adoption of the draft resolution A/80/L54 and to working with member states, UN system, regional organizations, and civil society toward the successful implementation of the International Decade of strengthening of peace for future generations. Distinguished colleagues, should a vote be requested, we kindly urge all delegations to support this initiative and vote in favor of the draft resolution. I thank you.

Madame President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. The Kingdom of Morocco is honored to introduce to the General Assembly today the draft resolution A/80/L76 entitled Global Conference on Promoting Interreligious and Intercultural Dialogue and Tolerance in Countering Hate Speech. This initiative is rooted in our collective commitment to address the alarming rise of intolerance and discrimination and scourge of hate speech. The draft decision builds upon General Assembly Resolution 77/318 and 79/316, both presented and sponsored by the Kingdom of Morocco and adopted by consensus, and which originally requested the Secretary-General to convene in 2025 a global conference Conference aimed at advancing interreligious and intercultural dialogue and tolerance as effective means to counter hate speech and promote a culture of peace. As reflected in the Secretary-General's letter of May 8th, 2026, circulated by the President of General Assembly on May 13th, 2026, the conference couldn't be convened in 2025, owing to the liquidity constraints currently affecting the organization. Today, the draft decision before the General Assembly seeks to provide a practical and timely way forward by deciding that the conference be convened on 17 September 2026, prior to the High-Level Week of the General General Assembly. This stage would allow for broad participation by member states, United Nations entities, religious leaders, civil society representatives, and other relevant stakeholders. The draft before us is purely procedural, limited in scope, and intended solely to facilitate the implementation of mandates already agreed by the General Assembly. The draft decision also acknowledges Morocco's continued commitment to supporting the successful organization of the conference, consistent with its longstanding efforts to promote dialogue among cultures and religions, mutual respect, and the values of peace and coexistence. Madame President, a time when hate speech, intolerance, and discrimination can continue to pose serious challenges to social cohesion and international peace, the convening of this conference will provide an important platform for strengthening collective action and fostering understanding among people, cultures, and civilizations. Thus, this initiative reflects the farsighted leadership of His Majesty King Mohammed King Mohammed VI, the Commander of the Faithful, may God assist him, who has consistently placed dialogue among cultures and religion at the heart of Morocco's engagement on the international stage. Guided by the principles of moderation, openness, and mutual respect, His Majesty has championed numerous efforts aimed at fostering understanding among people, promoting peaceful coexistence and preserving the shared values that unite humanity. Morocco's sponsorship of this initiative is therefore a natural extension of the Kingdom's longstanding commitment and the royal vision of His Majesty King Mohammed VI to advancing a culture of peace and countering the forces against hatred, division, and inacceptance of the other through dialogue and cooperation. In closing, The Kingdom of Morocco wishes to express its appreciation to the Secretary-General and to the President of General Assembly for their cooperation in rescheduling this event. We invite all member states to join us in supporting this decision, reaffirming our shared resolve to promote a culture of peace, coexistence, and mutual respect.

We thank you.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Under President Trump's leadership, the United States is returning the United Nations to its core purposes: maintaining international peace and security and fostering cooperation among sovereign nations, as well as delivering measurable results, not ideological statements. Resolutions must be concise and actionable, They should drive outcomes, not just fill calendars. We urge member states to exercise restraint. Filling the agenda with symbolic observances diverts attention from the UN's essential work. The unchecked growth of reports, conferences, and hollow negotiations has strained resources and eroded global confidence. For these reasons, the United States cannot support this resolution. We call for a renewed commitment to focused diplomacy and results-oriented action to restore this institution's credibility. The United States would also like to make points of clarification on language contained in the resolution. We underscore that UN General Assembly resolutions are non-binding documents that do not create rights or obligations under international law. The United States remains vigilant against attempts to inject ideological or vague language into UN resolutions. The terms used in this resolution, such as culture of peace and intergenerational dialogue, lack clear definitions and often serve as tools for soft governance that impinge upon state sovereignty. We continue to assert that technical assistance and UN programs should be based on objective criteria, not inconsistent labels. Additionally, we find the focus on future generations in this context to be performative rather than practical. While we support the needs of youth, we will not tolerate attempts to introduce harmful gender ideology or controversial terminology under the guise of social cohesion and sustainable development. Finally, we would like to highlight paragraph 31 of UNGA Resolution 79/327 that, that notes concern with the significant increase in the number of proposals to proclaim international days, weeks, months, years, or decades on a trial basis, to put on hold consideration of new proposals for international days, weeks, months, years, and decades during the 81st and 82nd sessions. This is the kind of efficient reform this institution should champion. For these reasons, the United States cannot support this resolution.

Thank you.
